principles.definition_ops: Time actions in seconds using a stopwatch or metronome before drawing to establish the rhythm. Use 12 frames per step for a normal walk, 6 frames for a run, and 4 frames for a fast run.
Create easing by spacing inbetween drawings progressively closer together as they approach or leave an extreme pose. Use this cushioning to indicate mass slowing down or starting up.
Plot the path of action for all joints and extremities to ensure they follow smooth, continuous arcs or figure-8 patterns. Avoid linear movement unless depicting a forceful, mechanical strike.
Draft the storytelling keys and extremes first to map the scene's structure. Animate straight ahead over these guideposts, handling one specific body part at a time to retain spontaneous flow.
Elongate the character's shape to bridge gaps during fast movements, simulating a transparent motion blur. Compress the volume immediately upon contact to amplify the impact.
Drag extremities like hands and feet behind the leading joints to create overlapping action. Break the joints in motion to make straight limbs appear limber and flexible.
Construct figures from the inside out using 3D masses rather than drawing flat, graphic outlines. Ensure structural balance by naturally opposing the angles of the pelvis and shoulders.
Amplify the highest and lowest points of a character's mass during movement to impart a believable sense of weight. Exaggerate pose contrast far beyond what a rotoscoped live-action frame provides.
Add a preparatory movement in the opposite direction before a primary action to signal intent to the viewer. Place this anticipation as a distinct extreme pose on your exposure sheet.
Animate clothing, hair, and soft tissue so they move in the opposite vertical direction of the main body mass. Delay these elements slightly so they offset the primary timing and add richness.
Design storytelling key poses that communicate the specific action, attitude, and emotion instantly. Ensure the silhouette is unmistakable and clearly readable before calculating any inbetweens.

Base the character's movement on distinct, recognizable personalities and emotions rather than generic mechanical formulas. Ground imaginative, wacky designs in believable physical weight and empathetic acting.
